title: Arithmetic Operators
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of arithmetic operators in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply arithmetic operators in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to numerical edge cases and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Arithmetic Operators through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding arithmetic operators helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Arithmetic Operators helps you reason about addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Then connect it to Remainder and exponentiation. The remaining syllabus points—Numerical edge cases—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports arithmetic operators. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for arithmetic operators using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Numerical edge cases), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain arithmetic operators, identify its place in data types, literals, and operators, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
